pending_articles.title: Deciphering auditory neuroprogenitor stemness for large-scale neuronal screening
pending_articles.content: Sensorineural hearing loss can arise from damage to sensory hair cells, auditory neurons or their synaptic connections, with auditory neuropathy and cochlear synaptopathy highlighting the importance of neural integrity for hearing. The mammalian cochlea has limited capacity to regenerate lost auditory neurons. Understanding the molecular programs that sustain cochlear progenitor expansion and neurogenic competence could support neuronal regeneration and provide renewable models for auditory drug discovery. We previously established that WNT activation combined with dual SMAD inhibition (CHIR-DS) supports scalable expansion and neuronal differentiation of mouse auditory neuroprogenitors (ANPGs). Here, we characterize the transcriptional, chromatin and metabolic changes associated with the induced state. RNA-seq and ATAC-seq identified reduced Id1 and Id2 expression and increased accessibility at proneural basic helix-loop-helix motifs, alongside transcriptional enrichment of translation, mTOR and glucose-metabolism programs. Compared with growth-factor controls, CHIR-DS-treated ANPGs showed slight increase in glycolysis at early passage. However, after long-term expansion, both glycolysis and mitochondrial respiration were markedly enhanced. Human fetal ANPGs also responded to CHIR-DS with increased sphere growth and retained neural differentiation capacity, providing proof of concept beyond the mouse system. Finally, neurons derived from stemness-induced ANPGs (siANs) supported a 384-well reporter assay and a 2,560-compound pilot screen that nominated candidate neurite-outgrowth enhancers. Together, these findings validate the pathway basis of ANPG stemness induction, characterize the resulting molecular and metabolic state, and demonstrate human feasibility and a neuronal screening application.
pending_articles.author: Rousset, F., Pepe, L., Sarhadi, M., Lemeille, S., Sgroi, S., Oberhauser, L., Daskalou, D., Ilmjarv, S., Braun, S., Senn, P.

pending_articles.title: A foundation model for brain organoid network dynamics uncovers intrinsic computation and convergent disease phenotypes
pending_articles.content: Brain organoids develop self-organizing neural networks that can be used to model neurodevelopment and disease. Here we introduce PULSE, a foundation model developed using over 900 hours of high-density microelectrode array recordings of in vitro and ex vivo neural tissue. We show that this single model can address two open questions: how disease-associated variants alter network development, and how naive circuits encode information. PULSE revealed accelerated network maturation in held-out human 16p11.2-deletion organoids. It also revealed a change in network coordination shared with SHANK3 deficiency. Because organoids develop without sensory input, they let us ask how circuits encode information before any representation is learned. Closed-loop control of a virtual inverted pendulum engaged existing spontaneous activity patterns rather than creating new ones. PULSE provides a common reference frame for neural circuits across genotypes, protocols and tasks.

pending_articles.title: Reuse of learned subtask representations during human planning
pending_articles.content: The notion of a compositional reuse of previously learned problem solutions predicts that the human brain should reinstate such learned subtask representations during planning. Here, we test this in a value-ranking task implemented in an online and a magnetoencephalography (MEG) experiment, respectively. Participants first learned pairwise rankings and subsequently solved problems where these learned rankings could either be reused or required reordering. Behaviourally, in the online experiment, we show the availability of a reusable subtask structure improved accuracy, with computational modelling indicating a greater weighting of subtask-level value when participants could avail of this learnt structure. In MEG, during planning, we show enhanced reactivation of task-relevant subtask representations in the reusable condition, and particularly so early in the experiment. In a subsequent probe task, we show subtask-identity representations generalised to a novel context and that stimuli belonging to the same learned subtask manifest an increase in their neural similarity. Temporally delayed linear modelling (TDLM) revealed forward and backward sequential reactivation at a subtask level, alongside backward stimulus-level replay, with subtask sequenceness varying according to task context. The findings provide convergent behavioural, computational and neural evidence for reactivation and reuse of learnt relational structures for novel problem solving.

pending_articles.title: Linking anterior cingulate sulcal variability to attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder behavior
pending_articles.content: Background: The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) is consistently implicated in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). ACC variability, including its most variable structure, the paracingulate sulcus (PCGS), has been known since the late 1800s, and since then, has been linked to cognitive control, impulsivity, and psychiatric conditions comorbid with ADHD, including autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia. Yet, the role of the PCGS in ADHD remains unexamined at the individual level. Methods: We characterized PCGS incidence, asymmetry, and morphology in 247 children and adolescents (144 ADHD: 10.9 +/- 2.73 years old, 75% male; 103 neurotypical: 12.2 +/- 3.17 years old, 50% male) from the ADHD-200 dataset. The PCGS was manually identified in FreeSurfer cortical surface reconstructions. Morphometric measures, including sulcal length, depth, and cortical thickness, were extracted and normalized to hemisphere-wide variables. Between-group analyses tested whether PCGS presence, asymmetry, and quantitative morphology differed by diagnosis, while behavioral analyses examined associations with inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity, and cognitive measures. Age and gender were included as covariates. Results: Analyses revealed that, in both NT and ADHD individuals, there was significant leftward asymmetry in PCGS presence. Between groups, the PCGS was less likely to be present in individuals with ADHD in the left hemisphere. Leftward PCGS absence was also associated with significantly higher ADHD index and hyperactivity-impulsivity scores. Conclusions: These findings advance understanding of how early neurodevelopmental variation in cortical folding may serve as a structural intermediary between genetic liability and the behavioral expression of ADHD.

pending_articles.title: Lysosomal Glycosaminoglycan Catabolism Regulates Microglial Cell State in the Developing CNS
pending_articles.content: Remodeling of the extracellular matrix (ECM), a complex structural and signaling network of the nervous system, is essential for CNS development, plasticity, and injury responses, yet how individual neural cell types contribute to this process remains poorly understood. Here, we show that phagocytic clearance of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), major components of the ECM, is an intrinsic function of microglia in the developing CNS. Our studies reveal an unexpected finding that impaired GAG clearance shifts microglia toward a non-homeostatic cell state seen in immature and disease-associated microglia (DAM), supporting a reciprocal relationship between the ECM and microglia. Using mouse models of Mucopolysaccharidosis VII, we examined the consequences of deleting {beta}-glucuronidase (GUSB), a lysosomal enzyme required for GAG degradation. Loss of GUSB causes early accumulation of undegraded chondroitin sulfate within microglial lysosomes, as confirmed by LC-MS analysis of intracellular GAGs isolated from cortical microglia. Single-cell RNA sequencing identified Gusb-null microglia as a distinct transcriptional population enriched for a core transcriptome shared by immature and disease-associated microglia. Together, these findings establish lysosomal GAG catabolism as a pathway that links ECM remodeling to the acquisition of adult homeostatic microglial identity during CNS development.

pending_articles.title: Oligodendrocyte stress response as a driver of vascular dementia
pending_articles.content: Vascular dementia (VaD) is a prevalent and devastating neurocognitive disorder characterized by profound white matter damage, yet the precise cellular mechanisms linking cerebrovascular stress to demyelination remain poorly understood. Here, we characterize the impact of a chronic cardiometabolic stress regimen combining a high-fat diet and hypertension (HF/HBP) on central nervous system structure and function. Adult HF/HBP mice exhibit progressive oligodendroglial cell loss and myelin thinning, followed by cognitive impairments, anxiety-like behavior, and memory deficits that recapitulate clinical features of VaD. Mechanistically, we identify the integrated stress response (ISR) as a central driver of this pathology; pharmacological inhibition of the ISR restores myelination, while cell-specific genetic deletion of the ISR-activating kinase PERK from oligodendrocytes fully protects mice from HF/HBP-induced pathological and behavioral defects. Furthermore, we provide translational evidence that the ISR is activated in oligodendrocytes in human cases of cerebrovascular disease. Together, these findings reveal a critical, cell-autonomous role for oligodendroglial ISR activation during cerebrovascular stress and position this pathway as a viable therapeutic target to mitigate VaD pathogenesis.

pending_articles.title: High-throughput light-sheet 3D microscopy of whole rodent brain microstructure for integration with MRI
pending_articles.content: Whole-brain cellular mapping is essential for understanding how differences in cellular architecture shape brain organisation and function. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) provides whole-brain coverage in humans and animal models but is only indirectly sensitive to cellular features. Integrating MRI with whole-brain microscopy is therefore critical for interpreting existing microstructural MRI metrics and developing new, more specific ones. Here, we present a scalable cross-resolution framework that integrates 3D light-sheet microscopy (LSM) of intact rodent brains with diffusion MRI (dMRI) to bridge cellular and macroscopic brain imaging. By combining active electrotransport-based tissue clearing and immunolabelling with accelerated LSM acquisitions, we achieve whole-brain multiplexed mapping of neuronal and glial populations in intact rodent brains on timescales comparable to conventional histology and 2D microscopy. This throughput enables LSM and MRI integration at scale, linking macroscopic MRI contrasts to microscopic cellular features within the same tissue. We apply this framework across eight genetically diverse mouse strains to develop predictive models of 3D microscopy-derived cellular features from multi-shell dMRI-derived contrasts. We demonstrate that data-driven combinations of state-of-the-art dMRI contrasts predict neuronal and astrocytic features better than individual contrasts, across all animals. Our novel approach enables 3D microscopy to guide the development and interpretation of microstructural MRI measures that are ultimately translatable to the living human brain.

recently_processed.title: Intersectional genetic targeting of molecularly distinct melanin-concentrating hormone neuron subpopulations reveals distinct and overlapping subcircuit architecture
recently_processed.content: The lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) coordinates crucial and innate behaviors through heterogeneous yet poorly understood neuronal populations and circuits. Neurons that produce melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH; encoded by the Pmch gene) are primarily localized in the LHA and contribute to feeding, sleep-wake regulation, memory, and reward-associated behaviors. Building on foundational anatomical studies, our single-cell transcriptomic analysis of the LHA identified markers distinguishing at least two transcriptionally distinct MCH subpopulations. These subpopulations are distinguished by the selective enrichment of the Tacr3 and Cartpt transcripts, with each comprising approximately half of the total MCH population. However, these subpopulations remain poorly understood owing to limited genetic targeting tools. We hypothesized that MCH neurons operate through functionally distinct, parallel subcircuits that exhibit unique neuroanatomical projections. In this study, we leveraged Pmch and Tacr3 expression to intersectionally dissociate these neurons into Type I MCH (Pmch+/Tacr3+) and Type II MCH (Pmch+/Tacr3-) subpopulations. We first validated a Tacr3-Flpo mouse line for the genetic targeting of the Type I MCH subpopulation. We then generated an intersectional Type I MCH neuron reporter line to visualize Type I axonal projections. In parallel, we injected a dual recombinase mouse line with the intersectional genetic targeting viruses, Conditional Viral Expression by Ribozyme Guided Degradation (ConVERGD), and identified overlapping and distinct projections by Type I and Type II MCH neurons using fluorescence microscopy, super-resolution imaging, and high-spatial resolution fiber mapping. Overall, these data establish the first subpopulation-resolved anatomical framework for molecularly distinct Type I and Type II MCH subcircuits, thus establishing a foundation for future circuit-level functional studies.

recently_processed.title: Neuronal FICD shapes motivated behavior through modulation of dopamine receptor dynamics
recently_processed.content: Motivated behaviors rely on dopaminergic signaling, which in turn depends on the correct folding and trafficking of receptors through the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Within the ER, the AMPylase enzyme FICD acts as a molecular rheostat through its modification of the chaperone BiP, dynamically tuning the organelle's responsiveness to folding perturbations and cellular stress. While the biochemistry of FICD is well-established, its role in complex animal behavior remains poorly understood. Here, we identify FICD as a conserved contributor to the generation of motivated behavior. In Drosophila, pan-neuronal knockdown of dFic significantly reduces feeding, spontaneous locomotion, and reward-seeking behavior. These alterations occur without disrupting circadian architecture, motor capacity, or homeostatic hunger, indicating a specific loss of motivational drive. Depleting dFic within subsets of dopamine receptor-expressing (Dop1R1) neurons recapitulates these behavioral alterations. Transcriptomic profiling reveals that dFic depletion does not induce a canonical unfolded protein response, pointing to a specific post-transcriptional alteration rather than global ER stress. At the molecular level, dysregulated dFic alters the localization and abundance of Dop1R1. Finally, we demonstrate that this regulatory axis is evolutionarily conserved, as loss of FICD similarly diminishes motivated behaviors in C. elegans and mice. Together, these findings implicate FICD in the generation of motivated behavior and link dynamic control of ER proteostasis to dopamine-receptor maturation.
recently_processed.author: Weaver, K. J., Abdon, B., Toth, B., Jack, A., Giblin, W., Burgess, C. R., Pletcher, S. D., truttmann, m. c.

recently_processed.title: Criticality-related dynamics accompany long-term functional decline in primary cortical MEA cultures
recently_processed.content: Primary cortical neuron cultures are widely used to study network development and decline, but their long-term electrophysiological trajectories are poorly characterized. We used multi-electrode arrays to longitudinally monitor Wistar rat cortical cultures for up to ~730 days in vitro (DIV), combining activity measures with survival analysis and criticality metrics. Wells shared an early developmental phase, with mean firing rate peaking at 12-14 Hz around DIV 100-150, before diverging into two phenotypes: early-death wells, showing progressive loss of burst organization, longer inter-burst intervals, shorter bursts, and steep declines in active-electrode recruitment; and long-survival wells, which sustained organized bursting and measurable activity well beyond DIV 400, in some cases past DIV 700. Cox proportional-hazards modeling with FDR correction across thirteen candidate features identified burst duration, inter-burst interval, synchrony, mean firing rate, branching ratio, and Kappa index as significant predictors of time to network failure. Criticality metrics offered the most mechanistic insight: in early-death wells, branching ratio declined toward zero and Kappa index rose toward its upper bound as networks approached silencing. Beyond their average levels, the rate of change of branching ratio and Kappa index over recordings was the strongest correlate of survival time among all criticality metrics. Neuronal avalanche size and duration exponents and their scaling relation, remained consistent with scale-free dynamics in both phenotypes while networks were active, though avalanche occurrence rate declined progressively in early-death wells without reaching significance as an independent predictor. These results show that long-term network survival is not determined by firing rate alone, but by preserved burst organization, sustained electrode recruitment and near-critical propagation dynamics. This work offers one of the longest electrophysiological characterizations of rodent cortical cultures to date and identifies criticality-based metrics as promising tools for predicting network decline and evaluating interventions to preserve long-term neuronal function.

recently_processed.title: A human model of the neurodevelopmental metabolic shift
recently_processed.content: The neurodevelopmental metabolic shift transitions the energy sources and metabolic pathways used by neurons to critically support survival, growth, and the timing of functional maturation. To better understand metabolic regulation during human neuronal development, and to facilitate the study of early neurodevelopmental disorders impacting this time window, establishing a combination of effective human model systems will be required. We report that a streamlined strategy using genetic induction of neuronal differentiation by NGN2 expression recapitulates hallmarks of metabolic reprogramming associated with neuronal maturation. The approach is refined to increase the uniformity of differentiation, allowing reproducible high-throughput assessments. We validate appropriate readouts of metabolic function, including gene expression, cellular respiration, and mitochondrial imaging which can be combined to present a cohesive assessment of metabolic status and reliance on oxidative phosphorylation relative to glycolysis. Collectively, the strategy presented will enhance the ability of investigators to gather foundational and disease-related insights into regulatory mechanisms of the metabolic shift critical to successful neuronal differentiation.
recently_processed.author: Pettit, S. N., Kornfeld, A. T., Morales, C., Meffert, M. K.

recently_processed.title: Identification of Synchronously Active Cells (ISAC) to study the activity of cell assemblies
recently_processed.content: Cell assemblies--groups of neurons that fire synchronously--are central to neuronal computation. Technological advances now permit the simultaneous recording of large neuronal populations; however, many existing cell assembly detection algorithms rely on simplified measures such as pairwise correlations, failing to capture higher-order synchrony and thereby missing a rich repertoire of assemblies present in the data. To address these limitations, we developed Identification of Synchronously Active Cells (ISAC), which performs a rigorous, iterative search across all recorded units, leveraging the full dimensionality of the dataset to detect groups that fire together above chance. Using simulated recordings with ground-truth assemblies of increasing complexity, we demonstrate that ISAC considerably outperforms currently used algorithms in identifying synchronously active cells. Finally, we show that applying ISAC to experimental recordings uncovers novel features of assembly formation and dynamics. The power and sensitivity of ISAC can thus enable insights that remain inaccessible with existing methods.

recently_processed.title: Intranasal L-MYC Neural Stem Cells Restore Neurovascular and Neuroimmune Homeostasis After TBI via CX3CL1 Upregulation and ICAM-1 Downregulation
recently_processed.content: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) triggers persistent neuroimmune and neurovascular dysfunction that contributes to secondary brain injury and limits recovery. Here, we investigated whether a single intranasal dose of LMNSC01 could reprogram neuroinflammatory and neurovascular responses post TBI and whether these effects were conserved across biological sex. Immunocompetent male and female rats underwent a controlled cortical impact (CCI) or Sham surgery and 7 days later received a single bolus dose of LMNSC01 (6 x10^6 cells/dose) or vehicle. Integrated histological and transcriptomic analyses and multiplex tissue ELISA were used to characterize injury- and treatment-associated responses. CCI induced persistent but sex-dependent transcriptional changes. Male rats exhibited prominent innate immune, adhesion, extracellular matrix, and tissue remodeling responses, whereas females demonstrated broader activation of microglial, interferon, complement, MHC/antigen presentation, and humoral/adaptive immune pathways. LMNSC01 treatment reprogrammed these distinct injury states through partially sex-specific mechanisms. In males, LMNSC01 increased endogenous immune-regulatory mediators, including Il1rn, and reduced pathways associated with adhesion and immune cell trafficking. In females, treatment decreased expression of genes related to microglial, leukocyte, MHC/antigen presentation, cytokine, and adhesion pathways, and reduced macrophage- and CD45 positive cell signatures. Despite these sex-dependent transcriptional changes, LMNSC01 produced conserved protein changes in both sexes, reducing injury associated ICAM-1 and restoring CX3CL1 proteins, proposing a novel molecular mechanism of LMNSCs modulating endothelial activation and neuron-microglia communication post injury. Our study provides further insight into sex differences in responses to injury and treatment after TBI and highlights candidate repair mechanisms, supporting further development of LMNSC01 as a minimally invasive therapy for TBI.

recently_processed.title: A rapid, genetically-tractable human iPSC-derived model for studying tissue-resident macrophage biology in Alzheimer's and other diseases
recently_processed.content: Large-scale genetic and preclinical studies strongly implicate myeloid cells, particularly brain-resident macrophages, in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Efferocytic clearance of apoptotic cells and other cholesterol-rich cellular debris is a core macrophage function and represents an active area of AD research. However, human tissue-resident macrophages remain difficult to model in vitro as they acquire their transcriptional and functional identities in response to signals from their host tissue microenvironment. Many existing differentiation protocols mimic human brain macrophage developmental trajectories, but these protocols rely either on multi-step cytokine cocktails and lengthy differentiation or transduction of multiple transcription factors, both of which introduce variability and complicate genetic manipulation. To address these limitations, we developed a simplified protocol that generates high-purity (>90% CD45+CD11b+) human iPSC-derived macrophage-like cells (iMacs) from cryopreservable erythro-myeloid progenitor (EMP)-like intermediates in 19 days, including a final 7-day maturation step driven by macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF) alone. Transcriptomic profiling reveals that iMacs show enrichment for phagocytic and lysosomal programs, processes integral to efferocytosis. At both the transcriptional and protein level, iMacs have higher expression of scavenger receptors such as CD36, CD163 and MRC1, and of AD risk genes such as TREM2. Functionally, iMacs show enhanced phagocytic uptake of diverse substrates relative to iPSC-derived microglia, including carboxylated latex beads, zymosan, amyloid-{beta} 1-42, and amyloid-{beta} 1-40, and exhibit expanded lysosomal mass. Robust TREM2 expression and signaling make iMacs a sensitive platform for interrogating TREM2 biology, with markedly higher phosphorylation of SYK and PLC{gamma}2 in response to TREM2 engagement compared to iPSC-derived microglia. iMacs also tolerate lipid-mediated siRNA transfection with high survival and knockdown efficiency, enabling rapid genetic perturbation of AD risk genes. Together, these features make iMacs a practical, scalable, and genetically tractable human macrophage model for studying the regulation and cell biology of core macrophage functions that are known to play critical roles in AD, aging, and other disorders.
